segments.text: Bjarni kemur með skó. Hann gefur Sigga skó og Ástu skó. Skórnir eru nýir; börnin fara í skóna.

grammar.title: Hann sér hana · hann hjálpar henni
grammar.rule: Hann sér hana, en hann hjálpar henni. Guðrún gefur börnunum kerti.
grammar.note_en:
Case is the form a noun or pronoun takes to show its job in a sentence. The nominative normally names the subject, the person doing something; the accusative and dative can mark different kinds of object. An object is a person or thing connected to the action. English often uses the same object form in both jobs; Icelandic distinguishes them. Ásta sér mig means “Ásta sees me”, but Hún hjálpar mér means “She helps me”. Ég becomes mig after sér and mér after hjálpar. Þú likewise becomes þig or þér. In Ég hjálpa þér (“I help you”), þér is ordinary singular “you”; it is different from the formal subject þér used with the priest in chapter 8.

A verb governs a case: this means its object must use that case. Learn hjálpa + dative (“help”), svara + dative (“answer”) and fylgja + dative (“follow, go with”) as patterns, rather than translating an English preposition. Siggi hjálpar henni means “Siggi helps her”; Ásta svarar honum means “Ásta answers him”; Snati fylgir þér means “Snati follows you”. Compare the accusative in Ég sé þig (“I see you”). Neither meaning nor the object's position alone tells you its case: the verb matters.

Hann becomes honum, hún becomes henni, and all three plural pronouns þeir, þær and þau become þeim in the dative. Við becomes okkur and þið becomes ykkur; these two forms are also used in the accusative. Þið gefið okkur laufabrauð means “You give us leaf bread”; Við hjálpum ykkur means “We help you”. Pronouns replace names or noun phrases; henni can refer to Ásta, Helga or Guðrún when the surrounding sentences make that clear.

With gefa, “give”, there are two objects: the recipient, who gets something, is dative; the thing given is accusative. Guðrún gefur börnunum kerti means “Guðrún gives the children candles”. Börnunum is dative plural with the article, already met for location; it now marks the recipients. Siggi gefur Ástu kerti means “Siggi gives Ásta a candle”. Óðinn gefur úlfunum matinn means “Óðinn gives the wolves the food”: úlfunum is dative plural definite, matinn accusative singular definite. Contrast gefur, “gives”, with fær, “gets”: Snati fær enga skó means “Snati gets no shoes”. Fá takes the thing received in the accusative. Segja can also name a dative recipient: Hún segir honum orðið means “She tells him the word”.

The table compares accusative after sér with dative after hjálpar. It is a reference to the patterns used in the story, not a demand to memorize every form at once. The dative forms already used after prepositions remain the same: hjá henni means “beside her”, and frá honum means “from him”; segja frá honum means “tell about him”. The new point is that a verb can require the dative without any preposition.

Mig langar í kjöt means “I want some meat”. Treat mig langar í as a recognition phrase here: mig is the experiencer, rather than an ordinary nominative subject. Its full pattern comes later; no exercise asks you to build it. Skelfur means “shakes” in the tremor scene; this too is supplied for recognition. The narrative and Hallur's retelling stay in the present. Jólin koma aftur (“Christmas comes again”) establishes a future occasion for Þá segi ég ykkur frá Þór og hamrinum (“Then I will tell you about Þór and the hammer”). Segi remains a present form.

words_with_history.title: Orð með sögu
text: Afi segir „jól“ og opnar bókina. Hann segir frá Óðni. Séra Þorvaldur segir „jól“ og les í kirkjunni.
Ásta segir „jól“ og sér kerti og skó. Manga tekur matinn. Hér eru jól, og hér er fólkið.
words_with_history.note_en: Jól is older than the Christian celebration. The same word can call up old stories for afi, the Christian feast for the priest, and candlelight and shoes for Ásta. This is a contrast in associations, not in household religion.
